subject: Anthropology
title: Interviews and Life Histories
description: A quick, practical guide to Interviews and Life Histories.

hook.text: A grandmother tells her life story. In two hours, she reveals more than a hundred surveys ever could.

buildup.text: Anthropologists use in-depth interviews and life histories to capture individual experiences within cultural context.

discovery.text: Life histories reveal how broad social forces — war, migration, poverty — land on one specific human life.

twist.text: Memory is selective. People reshape their past to fit the present. The story is data, but so are the distortions.

climax.text: Interviews turn statistics into stories, giving human faces to the patterns that fieldwork uncovers.

punchline.text: Every life is an archive of its culture.

quiz.question: Why do anthropologists collect life histories?
options: To capture individual experiences within cultural context

details.summary: Interviews and life histories are core ethnographic methods. Structured interviews gather specific data, unstructured interviews follow conversation naturally, and life histories trace an individual's experience across time — revealing how cultural patterns are lived through personal stories.
details.whyItMatters: Interviews access people's own words, explanations, and interpretations. Life histories show how cultural forces shape individual trajectories, bridging the gap between abstract social structures and the messy reality of lived experience.
takeaways: Interviews range from structured data gathering to open conversation
Life histories trace individual experience across cultural time
These methods access people's own words and interpretations

faq.question: How do life histories contribute to anthropological knowledge?
faq.answer: Life histories show how individuals navigate cultural systems, resist or conform to norms, and experience historical changes. They reveal variation within cultures that generalizations miss. They humanize anthropological analysis by grounding theory in real people's lived experiences.

faq.question: What ethical issues arise in anthropological interviews?
faq.answer: Informed consent, confidentiality, power imbalances between researcher and subject, and the risk of exposing vulnerable people to harm through published accounts. Anthropologists must consider how their representations affect the people they study, especially marginalized communities.
